mekki-muskil:1-1.t:
بِسم الله الرَّحْمَن الرَّحِيم: The bāʾ of بِسم الله was given kasra so that its vowel would resemble its effect (it causes the genitive). It is also said that it was given kasra to distinguish between what causes the genitive (khafḍ) and can only be a particle, such as the bāʾ and the lām, and what causes the genitive yet may also be a noun, such as the kāf. The bāʾ and its sisters only came to govern the genitive because they have no meaning except in nouns, so they govern the case-inflection that occurs only in nouns, namely the genitive. Likewise the particles that make verbs jussive only came to govern the jussive (jazm) because they have no meaning except in verbs, so they govern the case-inflection that occurs only in verbs, namely the jussive.

The alif was dropped from the script in بِسم الله because of frequent usage. It is also said that it was dropped because the sīn was originally vowelled, since the original state of the sīn is to carry a vowel and its being vowelless is due to a cause that entered upon it. It is also said: because the bāʾ is constantly attached to this noun. If you write بِسم الرَّحْمَن or بِسم الْخَالِق, the alif is also dropped according to al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī, whereas al-Farrāʾ said it is dropped only in بِسم الله and nowhere else. If a genitive particle other than the bāʾ is prefixed to اسم الله, dropping the alif is not permitted according to anyone, as in your saying «لَيْسَ اسْم كاسم الله» (there is no name like the name of Allah) and «لإسم الله حلاوة» (the name of Allah has sweetness).

The position of بِسم is nominative according to the Basrans, by an implied (muḍmar) mubtadaʾ (subject), its implied form being "ابتدائي بِسم الله" (my beginning is with the name of Allah). On this view the bāʾ is attached (mutaʿalliq) to the khabar (predicate) whose place the bāʾ has taken, its implied form being "ابتدائي ثَابت" or "مُسْتَقر بِسم الله" (my beginning is established / settled with the name of Allah), or the like. It is not good to attach the bāʾ to the implied maṣdar (verbal noun), because it would then fall within its ṣila (complement), and the mubtadaʾ would remain without a khabar. The Kufans said: بِسم الله is in the position of the accusative by an implied verb, its implied form being "ابتدأت باسم الله" (I begin with the name of Allah); on this view the bāʾ is attached to the omitted verb.

The original form of اسم is سمو, and it is also said سمو [Translator's note: the two forms are written identically in the edition; presumably the vowelling سِمْو and سُمْو is meant]. According to the Basrans it is derived from سما يسمو (to be high); that is why the sīn is given ḍamma in its original form in سم, and it is also said that it is derived from سمي يُسمى, which is why the sīn is given kasra in سم. Then its final letter was dropped and its first letter made vowelless as a weakening (iʿlāl) that does not follow the analogical rule. Evidence for this is their saying سمي in the diminutive, and its plural أَسمَاء, and the plural of أَسمَاء is أسامي. According to the Kufans it is derived from السمة (the mark), since its bearer is known by it; its original form is وسم, then it was weakened by dropping the fāʾ (first radical), and the ʿayn (second radical) was given a vowel, again against the analogical rule. On their view it would have to be diminutivised as وسيسم, yet no one has said that, because the diminutive returns things to their origins. They have arguments that would take long to mention. Their view is stronger in meaning, while the view of the Basrans is stronger in morphology (taṣrīf).

The alif was dropped in the script from اسم الله for lightness. It is also said that it was dropped so that it would not resemble the spelling of اللات (al-Lāt) in the view of those who pause on it with tāʾ. It is also said: because of frequent usage. The same is the reason for dropping the alif of الرَّحْمَن.

The original form of the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is الاه (ilāh). Then the alif and lām (the definite article) entered, so it became الالاه; then the hamza was lightened by casting its vowel onto the first lām, then the first lām was assimilated into the second, and the assimilation (idghām) and the dropping became obligatory for the sake of veneration and magnification. It is also said that the hamza was simply dropped and the alif and lām were given in compensation for it, and both became permanent for veneration. It is also said that its original form is لاه, then the alif and lām entered upon it and became permanent for veneration, and assimilation became obligatory because the first of the two identical letters is vowelless. Evidence for this is their saying «لهي أَبوك», meaning «لله أَبوك» (to Allah [belongs] your father [i.e. how excellent your father is]): they moved the ʿayn into the position of the lām because of their frequent use of it. Also evidence for it is the poet's saying: «لاه ابْن عمك» (by God [is] your cousin…), meaning لله.

Al-Zajjāj mentioned in some of his dictations (amālī) from al-Khalīl that its original form is ولاه, then the wāw was replaced with hamza, as in أشاح and وشاح. The alif in لاه is converted from a yāʾ; evidence for that is their saying «لهي أَبوك», where the yāʾ appears in place of the alif, which shows that the alif was originally yāʾ.

We have only treated these two nouns at length so that whatever resembles them, which we may neglect to mention, may be measured against them; and we will do likewise in everything that is like this, so know it.

السُّورَة (the sūra): its meaning may be "elevation", from سُورَة الْبناء (the course / tier of a building), as though it were a rank of honour; on this view it is not permitted to pronounce it with hamza. Its meaning may also be "a portion of the Quran", from your saying أسأرت فِي الْإِنَاء, i.e. "I left a remainder in the vessel"; on this view it is permitted to pronounce it with hamza. The Quran readers have agreed unanimously on not pronouncing it with hamza, so it admits both meanings.

mekki-muskil:2-2.t:
The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: {الْحَمد} is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), by ibtidāʾ (inchoation), and {وَللَّه} is the khabar (predicate). Ibtidāʾ is an abstract operator (ʿāmil maʿnawī) that is not pronounced: it is the noun that is the mubtadaʾ being free of verbal (pronounced) operators. Its accusative is permitted as a maṣdar (verbal noun).

The lām of لله was given kasra just as the bāʾ was in بِسم; the reason is the same. Sībawayh said that the original state of the lām is to be with fatḥa, as shown by its taking fatḥa with a pronoun, and pronominalisation returns things to their origins; it was given kasra only with an overt noun to distinguish it from the lām of emphasis (lām al-taʾkīd). Abū Muḥammad [Makkī] said: there is something to be examined in this, which would take long to mention. The lām is attached (mutaʿalliq) to the omitted khabar whose place it has taken, just as the bāʾ was in بِسم الله; its implied form is "الْحَمد ثَابت لله" (praise is established for Allah), or "مُسْتَقر" (settled), and the like.

The accusative of رب الْعَالمين is permitted as a vocative, or as praise (al-madḥ); its nominative is also permitted on the reading "هُوَ رب الْعَالمين" (He is the Lord of the worlds). ملك يَوْم الدّين is likewise like it. يَوْم الدّين is an adverb (ẓarf) treated as an object by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa); that is why ملك is made muḍāf to it (genitive construct). The same holds in the reading of whoever read مَالك with alif. As for whoever reads مَالك, a direct object must be assumed to be omitted, its implied form being "مَالك يَوْم الدّين الْفَصْل وَالْقَضَاء" (Master, on the Day of Judgement, of the decision and the judgement) and the like, because it is transitive. [Translator's note: the two readings are written identically in the edition; the second is presumably the reading treated as an active participle taking an object, as opposed to the first treated as a genitive construct.]

The plural of مَالك is ملاك and ملك; the plural of ملك is أَمْلَاك and ملوك. Abū ʿAmr read ملك with the lām made vowelless, just as one says فَخذ and فخذ; its plural on this view is أملك and ملوك. The accusative is also permitted in ملك as a ḥāl (circumstantial), or as a vocative, or as praise, or as a naʿt (adjective) of رب in the view of whoever puts it in the accusative.

We only mention these aspects so that the workings of i'rab and its analogical measures may be known, not so that it may be recited thus; for it is not permitted to recite except by what has been transmitted and authenticated from the well-known trustworthy authorities, from the Companions and the Successors, may Allah be pleased with them, and agrees with the script of the Muṣḥaf.

mekki-muskil:5-5.t:
The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: {إياك نعْبد}. ايا, according to al-Khalīl and others, is a pronoun (ism muḍmar) made muḍāf (genitive construct) to the kāf; this is anomalous (shādhdh), as no other pronoun is known to have been made muḍāf. Ibn Kaysān reported that the kāf is the noun, and ايا was brought in so that the kāf could lean on it, since it cannot stand by itself. Al-Mubarrad said: ايا is a vague noun (ism mubham) made muḍāf for specification; yet no other indeclinable vague noun is known to have been made muḍāf, and it is a principle of the vague noun that when it is made muḍāf it is indefinite and declinable, as with غير, بعض and كل. The Kufans said: إياك as a whole is a pronoun; yet no other pronoun is known whose ending changes, so that you say in it إِيَّاه, إِيَّاهَا and إِيَّاكُم. It is accusative by نعبد, a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) placed first; had it come later it would not be detached but would become an attached kāf, and you would say نعبدك.

His words {نستعين}: its pattern is نستفعل and its original form is نستعون, because it is from العون (help). The vowel of the wāw was cast onto the ʿayn, so the ʿayn took kasra and the wāw became vowelless, and it turned into yāʾ because of the kasra before it, since in the speech of the Arabs there is no vowelless wāw preceded by kasra, nor a vowelless yāʾ preceded by ḍamma. It was only weakened because the past tense is weakened. The maṣdar (verbal noun) is استعانة, originally استعوان: the vowel of the wāw was cast onto the ʿayn, the wāw was turned into alif, and one of the two alifs was dropped because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — some say the first, some say the second — and the hāʾ (tāʾ marbūṭa) was added in compensation for what was dropped. It is permitted to give kasra to the nūn, the tāʾ and the alif at the beginning of this verb and of its like outside the Quran; that is not good with the yāʾ.

His words, Majestic and Exalted: {اهدنا} is a request and petition; it is treated in i'rab like the imperative. However, it is indeclinable (mabnī) according to the Basrans, the dropping of the yāʾ from it being indeclinability, and declinable according to the Kufans, the dropping of the yāʾ from it being the jussive. The alif is a connective alif (alif al-waṣl), given kasra at the beginning of speech because it and what follows it are vowelless, since it was brought in only so that speech may begin with it and has no share of the vowels. It is also said that it was given kasra because of the kasra of the third letter. It was not given ḍamma because of the heaviness of moving from ḍamma to kasra, and it was not given fatḥa so that it would not resemble the alif of the first person. This is the reason for the connective alif wherever it occurs in verbs and nouns. If the third letter of the verb has ḍamma, the alif takes ḍamma by assimilation (itbāʿ): its vowel is for the meeting of two vowelless letters, and ḍamma was chosen because the third letter has ḍamma, as in ادخل and اخْرُج. As for the connective alif that comes with the lām of definiteness, in الرجل and الْغُلَام, it takes fatḥa at the beginning of speech to distinguish its entering on verbs and nouns from its entering on particles. اهدنا takes two objects, and it is permitted to confine it to one of them; here they are نَا and الصِّرَاط.

mekki-muskil:6-6.t: His words {الْمُسْتَقيم}: its original form is المستقوم, and its weakening (iʿlāl) in the noun and the maṣdar (verbal noun) is like the weakening of نستعين.

mekki-muskil:7-7.t:
His words {صِرَاط الَّذين} is a badal (substitute) for the first الصِّرَاط. الَّذين is a vague (mubham), indeclinable (mabnī), incomplete noun that requires a ṣila (relative clause) and a resumptive pronoun (ʿāʾid). It is not declined in the singular and the plural, but it is declined in the dual because the dual is sound, since it does not vary and occurs across all nouns in only one pattern; the plural is not like that. The reason for the indeclinability of الَّذِي is that it resembles the particles through its vagueness and its applying to everything, so it was denied case-inflection just as the particles are denied it. It is also said that it was made indeclinable only because it is incomplete and requires a ṣila, so it is like part of a noun, and part of a noun is always indeclinable, since case-inflection only occurs at the ends of nouns and verbs. It has also been said that الَّذين is a noun of plurality (ism jamʿ) and not a plural.

The singular of الَّذين is لذ, like عم and شج. When the alif and lām entered it and became permanent, the yāʾ returned, as it returns in قَاض, so you said الَّذِي. Its original form is to be written with two lāms, but they dropped one of the two lāms because of frequent usage, for lightness, and the plural followed the singular since it is indeclinable like it, being closer to it in case-inflection; the dual was written with two lāms according to the original.

The ṣila of الَّذين is His words أَنْعَمت عَلَيْهِم, and the hāʾ and mīm (the pronoun) refer back to them.

His words {غير المغضوب عَلَيْهِم}: غير is a vague noun, except that it is declined because it is constantly muḍāf (in genitive construct). Its genitive is as a badal for الَّذين, or as a naʿt (adjective) of them, since they are not meant as specific individuals, so they are treated like an indefinite noun, and thus غير may be a naʿt for them. It is a principle of غير that it is indefinite even if it is made muḍāf to a definite noun, because it does not denote a specific thing. The accusative of غير has been transmitted from Ibn Kathīr and others; its accusative is as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the hāʾ and mīm in عَلَيْهِم, or from الَّذين, since their form is that of a definite noun. If you wish, you may make it accusative as a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) according to the Basrans, though the Kufans disallowed it because of the entry of لَا. And if you wish, you may make it accusative by an implied أَعنِي (I mean).

The second عَلَيْهِم is in the position of the nominative as the deputy agent (mafʿūl lam yusamma fāʿiluhu, i.e. nāʾib fāʿil) of المغضوب, because it means "those with whom [He] is angry". There is no pronoun in it, since it is only made transitive by a preposition, like مر بزيد (he passed by Zayd); that is why it was not put in the plural.

His words {وَلَا الضَّالّين}: لَا is redundant (zāʾida) for emphasis according to the Basrans, and in the sense of غير according to the Kufans. Among the Arabs are those who replace the vowelless letter that precedes a doubled letter with a hamza, saying وَلَا الضألّين; that is when it is an alif. Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī read thus. He wanted to give the alif a vowel because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, but it could not be given a vowel, so he replaced it with a letter akin to it, close to it in point of articulation, sturdier and stronger than it, namely the hamza. [Translator's note: the edition prints the hamzated form identically to the ordinary form, وَلَا الضَّالّين; the hamzated form الضألّين is evidently intended.]
